newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-YOUTH TRIUMPHS OVER EXPERIENCE AT WIMBLEDON.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-YOUTH TRIUMPHS OVER EXPERIENCE AT WIMBLEDON.

text.p: Youth triumphed over experience on Saturday when 16-year-old Martina Hingis beat Jana Novotna to become the youngest Wimbledon singles champion for 110 years.
The Swiss world number one fought back from a flying start by the 28-year-old Czech to wrap up the final 2-6 6-3 6-3.

Novotna, veteran of 12 Wimbledons and runner-up to Steffi Graf here in 1993, visibly tired in the tense third set as she raced about the court chasing Hingis's fierce ground strokes but hampered by a pulled abdominal muscle.
Britain's Lottie Dodd in flowing skirt and petticoats was the only younger singles champion, taking the title in 1887 at the age of 15.
Novotna, whose 1993 disappointment at throwing away a big third set lead, had her weeping on the Duchess of Kent's shoulder, kept a firm handle on her emotions on Saturday.
She laughed and joked with Hingis and officials as the Duke and Duchess came on to the court and smiled broadly as she accepted the runners-up plate.
"I'm so proud of you," the Duchess said as she handed it over.
Novotna came out for the match all serve-and-volley guns blazing and took the first four games with some sizzling shots at the net. Throughout the match she had 22 volley winners to Hingis's nine.
Hingis won only two points in her first two service games as she was punished for sticking to the baseline.
The Swiss, a former junior champion here and a doubles winner in 1996, was being made to look very ordinary.
"I felt like a beginner," Hingis said afterwards. "I did not play badly. She was just all over the net."
But the guile and grit that brought Hingis her first grand slam title at the Australian Open in January enabled her to begin to read Novotna's game and to counter it with lobs and passes.

She broke Novotna's serve in the sixth game of the second set and saved three break points in a marathon last game of the set in which she needed all her famed cool-headedness to convert her fifth set point with a sweetly-placed lob.
"It was very important for me to break her serve. I had had so few chances," she said.
It was never a case of Novotna choking as she had four years ago when she was 4-1 and 40-15 up in the third set against Graf, who could not defend her title this year because of surgery.
The Czech world number three won the first two games of the third set, but they were titanic tussles during which she had to save five break points and then convert a second against Hingis's serve.
The effort appeared to tell on Novotna who on Friday pulled out of the doubles to treat her strained muscle.
She became tired and flushed and later in the set needed some courtside attention from her trainer who dispensed pills and an ice-pack.
Hingis broke her serve the next game with a backhand pass and a flicked forehand on the run.

Hingis went on to win the next four games. As Novotna served at 3-5 down, the Swiss earned one match point with a lob. She lost it by returning wide. She volleyed down the line to earn another which she converted with a forehand winner.
"Two different players came together in this game," Hingis said. "She's aggressive, I'm defensive.
"I did it this time," the smiling teenager added graciously "She could win next time. She deserves to win this title."
Novotna said: "I came into the match with a pulled abdominal muscle. Unfortunately I had a bit of pain in the second set and it got worse and worse throughout the match."
